title.en: The Constitution of India: An Introduction

text.en: Your team is playing a close match. A player from the other side says she had already crossed into her area before she was caught. The captains and the referee check the rulebook. Everyone has agreed in advance to abide by it. Our Constitution is a rulebook of this kind for the whole country. Every Republic Day parade celebrates the day it came into effect. In this chapter we learn how it was made and what it says.

A constitution is the set of basic rules by which a country is governed. It says how the legislature, executive and judiciary are formed, what their powers are and what rights citizens have. The prime minister, the council of ministers and the judges all promise to follow its provisions. When it came into effect, our Constitution had 22 Parts and 8 Schedules, and it has been amended since. Its values and ideals usually form the basis of all the laws made later.
A Constituent Assembly of members representing India's diverse regions, professions and groups prepared the Constitution. Dr Rajendra Prasad was its Chairman, and the first draft was prepared by a Drafting Committee chaired by Dr B. R. Ambedkar. The Assembly discussed the draft clause by clause in public and sought opinion from citizens. It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into effect on 26 January 1950, which we celebrate as Republic Day. Women members such as Hansa Mehta spoke of complete equality with men in all spheres of life.
The ideals of the Indian freedom movement, such as liberty, equality and self-rule, were enshrined in the Constitution. The freedom struggle also answered many how and what questions, such as how powers should be divided between the Centre and the States and how to keep the legislature and judiciary separate. Ideas from India's civilisational heritage, such as dharma, duty and non-violence, found a place too. For instance, Fundamental Duties are part of it. The Constitution also learned from other countries' constitutions while fitting India's own needs.
The Preamble is the opening statement. It tells us the values the Constitution upholds. It declares India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic and promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity to all citizens. Sovereign means free from outside control. Secular means the State has no official religion and treats all faiths equally, and a person does not need permission from the State to practise their faith unless it harms others. Democratic means the people choose their rulers and hold them accountable. Republic means the head of state is elected and not hereditary. Equality before the law means no one is above the law and everyone is treated alike; Radha, Imon and Harpreet study in the same class regardless of religion or region.
Fundamental Rights are basic rights given to every citizen, and they are promises that must be kept: equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and the right to constitutional remedies, that is, to go to court if rights are violated. The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) show the social and economic vision of the framers: that everybody should have a good standard of living. They are goals that may take time to achieve, unlike Fundamental Rights, which can be demanded in court immediately. Fundamental Duties, in Part IV-A, were added in 1976. Citizens must respect the Constitution, the National Flag and the National Anthem, protect the environment and public property, and develop a scientific temper. The electoral system is laid down so that every eligible citizen may vote. In 2004 the Supreme Court recognised the right of a citizen to display the national flag with respect, after a citizen challenged a rule.
The Constitution can be amended, so it grows with changing times, but the basic ideals remain. It is not only a legal document but also a work of art, with beautifully illustrated pages. It is relevant even though it was written more than seventy years ago because its values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity do not become old.

problem.en: Match each statement with a Preamble value: All citizens are equal before the law; A person can freely practise any religion; India chooses its own laws without outside rule.

text.en: Equal before the law shows equality.
Freedom to practise religion shows secularism.
Making our own laws shows sovereignty.

prompt.en: Explain how the Constitution is like a rulebook and which values guide it.

requiredIdeas.en: It sets rules for government and rights for citizens.
The Preamble states values: justice, liberty, equality, fraternity.
Everyone including leaders must follow it.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking Fundamental Duties were there in 1950.

points.en: The Constitution is the supreme rulebook of India.
It was drafted by the Constituent Assembly and adopted in 1949, effective on 26 January 1950.
The Preamble states its core values.
Fundamental Rights are enforceable; Directive Principles are goals; Fundamental Duties came in 1976.
